title: Heat Made, Heat Lost, Set Point

scenes.tts: A desert iguana basking on a rock can end up warmer than you are. So what does cold-blooded mean? Body temperature could depend on the heat an animal makes, the heat it loses, or a controller. Metabolic rate is energy used per unit of time, and nearly all of it ends up as heat.
scenes.visual: Body box with unknown arrow in (heat made?), arrow out (heat lost?) and a gold controller? dial; iguana tag near or above 37 C; then metabolic rate chip and all becomes heat.

scenes.tts: Mammals and birds are endotherms. They warm themselves mainly with heat from their own metabolism, held in by insulation. Ectotherms, like the desert iguana, take their temperature mainly from outside, such as the sun or a warm rock. Ectotherm does not mean a cold animal.
scenes.visual: Two boxes: endotherm (inner metabolism chip, thick insulation outline), desert iguana (arrows in from sun and warm rock).

scenes.tts: Heat leaves the body by four routes. Radiation is emission and absorption of electromagnetic energy. Conduction passes heat through direct contact. Convection is transfer by moving air or water. Evaporation carries heat away as water turns to vapour. The first three run either way. Evaporation only removes heat, and it costs water.

scenes.tts: Plot an endotherm's resting metabolic rate against air temperature. Inside the thermo-neutral zone, the line is flat, at basal metabolic rate. Below the lower critical temperature, it climbs. Above the upper critical temperature, it rises again, as panting and sweating take work. In 1950, Scholander and Irving found that thick-furred arctic mammals stay flat into much colder air than tropical ones.
scenes.visual: Axes in this sketch; curve drawn left to right: climbs, flat zone, rises; critical temperatures marked; a second shallower curve for thick fur flat far further left.

scenes.tts: If body temperature and conductance stay roughly constant, the steepness of the cold limb equals thermal conductance, how readily heat leaks out per degree of difference. These numbers are invented for practice. A small endotherm holds thirty-seven degrees Celsius, with a conductance of zero point zero two zero watts per kelvin. At twenty-seven degrees, the gap is ten kelvin, so it makes zero point two zero watts. At seventeen degrees, the gap is twenty kelvin, so it makes zero point four zero watts. Fluff the fur until conductance halves, and that cost drops back to zero point two zero watts.
scenes.visual: Cold limb zoomed: line from the equation, W against air temperature; points at 27 and 17 degrees with drop lines; second line at half the slope returns 17 degrees to 0.20 W.
scenes.caption: If body temperature and conductance stay roughly constant, the steepness of the cold limb equals thermal conductance, how readily heat leaks out per degree of difference. These numbers are invented for practice. A small endotherm holds 37 degrees C, with a conductance of 0.020 W per K. At 27 degrees, the gap is 10 K, so it makes 0.20 W. At 17 degrees, the gap is 20 K, so it makes 0.40 W. Fluff the fur until conductance halves, and that cost drops back to 0.20 W.

scenes.tts: A set point is the value a control system defends. In fever, it is raised. In torpor, a bird or mammal's body temperature drops under control. In hibernating American black bears, metabolism fell to twenty-five percent of basal while body temperature stayed between thirty and thirty-six degrees Celsius. Cooling alone does not explain that. Keep one rule. For an endotherm at steady state, heat made equals heat lost, and the temperature it defends can shift, as in fever or torpor.
scenes.visual: Gold set-point line on a temperature scale rises (fever) and drops (torpor); then bear bars: 25% of basal with temperature band 30 to 36 C; cooling alone does not explain.

For an endotherm at steady state, heat made equals heat lost, and the temperature it defends can shift, as in fever or torpor.
